ourAnswer: The sugars carry many -OH groups (glucose five, sucrose eight) which hydrogen bond with water; cyclohexane and benzene are pure hydrocarbons with no H-bonding group, held only by van der Waals forces. Ring size is irrelevant.
note: No key in either stream. Grounded in the chapter's own glucose-pentaacetate evidence (p283), which is what establishes the five -OH groups.

ourAnswer: One molecule of D-galactose and one of D-glucose (equimolar).
note: No key. Grounded in 10.1.3(iii), which states lactose is composed of beta-D-galactose and beta-D-glucose linked C1-C4. The chapter never gives a sign of rotation for galactose, so none is claimed.

ourAnswer: Glucose exists as the cyclic hemiacetal; acetylation esterifies all five -OH groups including the anomeric -OH at C-1, which locks the ring shut so it can no longer reopen to the open-chain aldehyde. Hence no free -CHO is available and the pentaacetate gives no oxime.
note: No key. Grounded in the 'Cyclic Structure of Glucose' facts on p285, including the printed statement that the pentaacetate does not react with hydroxylamine.

ourAnswer: Amino acids exist as zwitter ions, so the crystal is held by strong ion-ion forces like a salt (high m.p.) and interacts with water by ion-dipole forces (high solubility). A halo acid has no basic group, cannot form an internal salt, and is held by weaker forces.
note: No key. Grounded in 10.2.2's printed statement that amino acids 'behave like salts rather than simple amines or carboxylic acids' because of the zwitter ion.

ourAnswer: The protein (albumin) is denatured and coagulates; the water is not lost but is trapped and adsorbed within the network of the coagulated protein, a little escaping as steam.
note: No key. HONEST LIMIT, and the weakest-grounded answer in the chapter: 10.2.4 states that coagulation of egg white on boiling is an example of denaturation, but it does NOT state where the water goes. The denaturation half is grounded; the fate of the water is inferred from it and is flagged as such rather than presented as the book's claim.

ourAnswer: Vitamin C is water soluble, so it is readily excreted in urine and cannot be stored (unlike the fat soluble A, D, E, K stored in liver and adipose tissue). It must be supplied regularly in the diet.
note: No key. Grounded almost verbatim in 10.4.1(ii).

ourAnswer: Thymine, beta-D-2-deoxyribose and phosphoric acid.
note: No key. Grounded in 10.5.1 (complete hydrolysis yields a pentose sugar, phosphoric acid and a base; DNA's sugar is beta-D-2-deoxyribose) and 10.5.2 (nucleotide = nucleoside + phosphate at 5').

ourAnswer: RNA is single stranded. Fixed base ratios follow from complementary pairing across two strands; their absence shows the bases are not paired one-for-one, so there is no complementary second strand.
note: No key. Grounded in 10.5.2, which states both the A-T / C-G pairing rule for the DNA double helix and that RNA's secondary structure is a single stranded helix.

ourAnswer: A carbohydrate that cannot be hydrolysed further to a simpler polyhydroxy aldehyde or ketone; e.g. glucose, fructose, ribose.
note: No UNIT 10 block in lech2an. Definition is verbatim from 10.1.1(i).

ourAnswer: Carbohydrates that reduce Fehling's solution and Tollens' reagent, i.e. those with a free aldehydic or ketonic group. All monosaccharides; among disaccharides, maltose and lactose. Sucrose is non-reducing.
note: No key. Grounded in 10.1.1 and 10.1.3.

ourAnswer: (i) Food/energy storage, as starch. (ii) Structural support, as cellulose in the cell wall.
note: No key. Grounded in 10.1.4(i)-(ii) and 10.1.5.

ourAnswer: Monosaccharides: ribose, 2-deoxyribose, galactose, fructose. Disaccharides: maltose, lactose.
note: No key. Each classification traceable to the chapter: ribose and 2-deoxyribose named as aldopentoses (p290), fructose a ketohexose (10.1.2.2), galactose a constituent of lactose (10.1.3 iii), maltose and lactose both described as disaccharides.

ourAnswer: The oxide linkage joining two monosaccharide units through an oxygen atom, formed by loss of a water molecule; e.g. C1 of alpha-D-glucose to C2 of beta-D-fructose in sucrose.
note: No key. Definition verbatim from 10.1.3.

ourAnswer: Glycogen is the animal storage polysaccharide ('animal starch'), structurally like amylopectin but more highly branched. Starch is the plant store and has TWO components, unbranched amylose (15-20%) and branched amylopectin (80-85%).
note: No key. Grounded in 10.1.4(i) and (iii).

ourAnswer: (i) Sucrose -> D-(+)-glucose + D-(-)-fructose (invert sugar). (ii) Lactose -> D-galactose + D-glucose.
note: No key. Rotation signs given only where the chapter itself prints them (glucose +52.5 deg, fructose -92.4 deg); none is asserted for galactose, which the chapter never gives.

ourAnswer: Starch is built from alpha-D-glucose (C1-C4 links, plus C1-C6 branches in amylopectin); cellulose is built only from beta-D-glucose in straight unbranched C1-C4 chains.
note: No key. Grounded in 10.1.4(i) and (ii).

ourAnswer: (i) HI -> n-hexane (straight six-carbon chain). (ii) Bromine water -> gluconic acid (carbonyl is aldehydic). (iii) HNO3 -> saccharic acid (primary -OH present).
note: No key. All three are the chapter's own numbered structural evidences 2, 4 and 6 for glucose (pp283-284), including what each reaction proves.

ourAnswer: Three: (i) no Schiff's test and no hydrogensulphite addition product with NaHSO3 despite an aldehyde group; (ii) the pentaacetate does not react with hydroxylamine; (iii) glucose exists in two crystalline forms, alpha (m.p. 419 K) and beta (m.p. 423 K). All are explained by the cyclic hemiacetal (pyranose) structure and its anomeric carbon.
note: No key. These are exactly the three facts the chapter itself lists under 'Cyclic Structure of Glucose' as not explicable by structure (I), with the melting points as printed.

ourAnswer: Non-essential = synthesised in the body (e.g. glycine, alanine); essential = not synthesised, must come from diet (e.g. valine, leucine). Ten of the twenty are essential.
note: No key. Definitions from 10.2.2; the examples are drawn from Table 10.2, where essential acids carry an asterisk (valine and leucine are asterisked; glycine and alanine are not). The count of ten is the chapter's own, stated in the Summary.

ourAnswer: (i) Peptide linkage: the -CO-NH- amide bond formed between -COOH and -NH2 with loss of water. (ii) Primary structure: the specific sequence of amino acids in each polypeptide chain. (iii) Denaturation: loss of native 3-D structure and biological activity on change of temperature or pH; secondary and tertiary structures destroyed, primary intact.
note: No key. All three definitions from 10.2.3 and 10.2.4.

ourAnswer: alpha-helix and beta-pleated sheet.
note: No key. Stated verbatim in 10.2.3(ii).

ourAnswer: Intramolecular hydrogen bonding, between the -NH of each residue and the C=O of a residue in the adjacent turn of the helix.
note: No key. Grounded in 10.2.3(ii)'s description of the alpha-helix.

ourAnswer: Fibrous: parallel chains held by hydrogen and disulphide bonds, fibre-like, insoluble in water; keratin, myosin. Globular: chains coiled into a spherical shape, usually water soluble; insulin, albumins.
note: No key. Grounded in 10.2.3(a) and (b), examples as printed.

ourAnswer: The zwitter ion carries both -COO- and -NH3+; with acid the -COO- accepts a proton, with base the -NH3+ loses one, so it reacts with both.
note: No key. Grounded in 10.2.2, which states 'In zwitter ionic form, amino acids show amphoteric behaviour as they react both with acids and bases.'

ourAnswer: Biocatalysts, almost all globular proteins; highly specific for reaction and substrate, needed in small quantities, and act by lowering activation energy (sucrose hydrolysis 6.22 kJ/mol by acid vs 2.15 kJ/mol by sucrase). Named after substrate or reaction, ending in -ase.
note: No key. Grounded in 10.3 and 10.3.1. NOTE A RATIONALISATION GAP, reported to the maintainer rather than bracketed: section 10.3.1 is TITLED 'Mechanism of Enzyme Action' and then never describes a mechanism - it ends on the dangling sentence 'Mechanism for the enzyme action has been discussed.' with no discussion, diagram or step anywhere. The answer therefore does not attempt a mechanism, because this edition of the chapter does not teach one.

ourAnswer: Secondary and tertiary structures are destroyed, primary structure remains intact, and the protein loses its biological activity (e.g. egg white coagulating, milk curdling).
note: No key. Stated almost verbatim in 10.2.4.

ourAnswer: By solubility: fat soluble (A, D, E, K) and water soluble (B group and C). Vitamin K is responsible for coagulation of blood.
note: No key. Classification from 10.4.1; vitamin K identified from Table 10.3, whose deficiency entry for K is 'Increased blood clotting time' - the only entry in that table touching blood coagulation.

ourAnswer: Both are essential because the body cannot synthesise them and deficiency causes disease: vitamin A - xerophthalmia and night blindness; vitamin C - scurvy. Sources: A from fish liver oil, carrots, butter and milk; C from citrus fruits, amla and green leafy vegetables.
note: No key. Diseases and sources taken directly from Table 10.3; the 'cannot be synthesised in our body' premise from 10.4.

ourAnswer: Long chain polymers of nucleotides (polynucleotides) present in chromosomes, of two kinds DNA and RNA. Functions: (i) heredity - DNA self-duplicates and passes identical strands to daughter cells; (ii) protein synthesis.
note: No key. Definition from 10.5, functions from 10.5.3.

ourAnswer: Nucleoside = base + pentose sugar (base at C-1'). Nucleotide = nucleoside + phosphoric acid esterified at C-5', i.e. base + sugar + phosphate.
note: No key. Both definitions verbatim from 10.5.2.

ourAnswer: Base pairing is specific - A only with T, C only with G - so each strand's sequence is fixed by the other's without being a copy of it. Hence complementary, not identical; this is what permits self-duplication.
note: No key. Grounded in 10.5.2's statement of the pairing rules and of why the strands are complementary.

ourAnswer: Structural: sugar deoxyribose vs ribose; fourth base thymine vs uracil; double stranded helix vs single strand. Functional: DNA is the chemical basis of heredity and self-duplicates; RNA (m-, r-, t-) carries out protein synthesis.
note: No key. Grounded in 10.5.1, 10.5.2, 10.5.3 and the chapter Summary, which states the same contrasts.

ourAnswer: Three: messenger RNA (m-RNA), ribosomal RNA (r-RNA) and transfer RNA (t-RNA).
note: No key. Stated verbatim in 10.5.2.
